questions.text:
Consider the following deterministic finite automaton (DFA)

The number of strings of length 8 accepted by the above automaton is _________
questions.solution:
Every path from the start reaches the final state after exactly 3 symbols (start [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] level 1 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] level 2 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] final, on either symbol at every step), and the final state loops on 0 and 1.

So every string of length [latex]\ge3[/latex] is accepted. Strings of length 8: [latex]2^8=256[/latex].

Answer: 256

questions.text: Let [latex]L_1[/latex] be a regular language and [latex]L_2[/latex] be a context-free language. Which of the following languages is/are context-free?
questions.solution:
Checking each statement:
- [latex]L_1\cap\overline{L_2}[/latex]: [latex]\overline{L_2}[/latex] need not be CFL [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] not always CFL.
- [latex]\overline{\overline{L_1}\cup\overline{L_2}}=L_1\cap L_2[/latex] (De Morgan) [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] CFL True
- [latex]L_2\cup\overline{L_2}=\Sigma^*[/latex], so the whole thing is [latex]\Sigma^*[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] CFL True
- [latex](L_1\cap L_2)\cup(\overline{L_1}\cap L_2)=L_2[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] CFL True

Answer: Options 2, 3 and 4

questions.text: Let [latex]L \subseteq \{0,1\}^*[/latex] be an arbitrary regular language accepted by a minimal DFA with k states. Which one of the following languages must necessarily be accepted by a minimal DFA with k states?
questions.solution:
For the complement, use the same DFA and swap final and non-final states. It has k states and is still minimal (any two states distinguishable for L are also distinguishable for its complement).

Adding or removing the single string 01, or computing L[latex]\cdot[/latex]L, can change the number of states.

Answer: [latex]\{0,1\}^*-L[/latex]

questions.text:
In a pushdown automaton [latex]P=(Q, \Sigma, \Gamma, \delta, q_0, F)[/latex], a transition of the form,

where [latex]p,q \in Q \; a \in \sigma \cup \{ \epsilon \} ,\;X,Y, \in \Gamma \cup \{ \epsilon \}[/latex], represents

[latex](q,Y) \in \delta(p,a,X)[/latex]

Consider the following pushdown automaton over the input alphabet [latex]\Sigma = \{a,b\}[/latex] and stack alphabet [latex]\Gamma = \{ \#, A\}[/latex].

The number of strings of length 100 accepted by the above pushdown automaton is ___________
questions.solution:
The PDA pushes # and then an A for every a; in q2 every b pops an A. It can reach the final state q3 only if an A is still on top.

So it accepts [latex]a^mb^n[/latex] with [latex]n \lt m[/latex]. For length 100: m + n = 100 with n [latex]\lt[/latex] m [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] n = 0, 1, [latex]\ldots[/latex], 49 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 50 strings.

Answer: 50

questions.text:
For a Turing machine M, < M > denotes an encoding of M. Consider the following two languages.

[latex]\begin{array}{ll} L1 = \{ \langle M \rangle \mid M \text{ takes more than } 2021 \text{ steps on all inputs} \} \\ L2 = \{ \langle M \rangle \mid M\text{ takes more than } 2021 \text{ steps on some input} \} \end{array}[/latex]

Which one of the following options is correct?
questions.solution:
In 2021 steps, M can read at most the first 2021 input symbols. So "more than 2021 steps" depends only on inputs of length up to 2021, a finite set.

Simulate M for 2022 steps on each such input; this decides both "on all inputs" (L1) and "on some input" (L2).

Answer: Both L1 and L2 are decidable

options: Both L1 and L2 are decidable.
